families.s: HSE control of slips on wet and contaminated food-production floors
families.t: water, food contamination, drainage, cleaning, floor roughness, footwear, spill response, obstructions
f: Slips and trips make up a substantial proportion of major injuries in food and drink manufacture.
Most sector slips occur on floors wet with water or contaminated with food product.
Most trips arise from obstructions or uneven surfaces.
Controls should first eliminate leakage, spillage and contamination at source.
Bunds, drainage channels and prompt spill treatment can protect walkways.
Floor surfaces should provide sufficient roughness for the expected contaminant.
Cleaning regimes should be checked because some treatments can increase slipperiness.
Suitable footwear and reduced pushing, pulling or load carrying can further reduce slip risk.

families.s: HSE prevention and mitigation of combustible food-dust explosions
families.t: DSEAR, flour, sugar, milk powder, dust clouds, ignition, extraction, venting, bonding and earthing
f: DSEAR requires assessment and protection where fire or explosion substances are handled or stored.
Combustible food dust can explode when its airborne concentration and an ignition source coincide.
Explosible examples include flour, sugar, instant coffee, dried milk and potato powder.
Milling, grinding, spray drying and grain transfer can generate explosive dust clouds.
Dust leakage and accumulation should be prevented by sealed systems and effective extraction.
Bins, silos and collectors may require properly designed explosion relief to a safe place.
Metal powder-handling systems and delivery tankers should be bonded and earthed against static discharge.
Hot work should be controlled by a permit system and ignition sources excluded from hazardous areas.

families.s: HSE safe design and movement of roll cages and wheeled racks
families.t: manual propulsion, visibility, stability, wheels, pushing, ramps, load height, maintenance
f: Fully loaded roll cages can weigh 500 kg or more and may obstruct the operator's view.
Injuries arise from pushing or pulling, overbalancing, repetitive loading and trapped hands or feet.
Roll cages can fall from vehicles or tail lifts during loading and unloading.
Frames and shelves should be robust enough for long-term use.
Larger wheels reduce the force needed to overcome small steps.
Castors, bearings and wheel materials should suit temperature, washing and floor conditions.
Workers should normally push one cage at walking speed and seek help on ramps or uneven surfaces.
Heavy goods should be placed low and loads should not exceed the load line or safe sight height.

families.s: HSE prevention of musculoskeletal disorders in food manufacture
families.t: repetition, lifting, cutting, packing, stacking, drinks containers, task design, mechanical aids
f: Food-sector musculoskeletal disorders include upper-limb disorders and back injuries.
Repetitive production-line work can cause persistent upper-limb disorders.
Repetitive or awkward lifting can cause chronic back pain.
High-risk tasks include cutting, boning, jointing and evisceration.
Packing and stacking boxes, crates, sacks and containers are common risk sources.
Handling casks, kegs and crates creates heavy manual-handling demands.
HSE case studies show mechanical transfer equipment can virtually eliminate repetitive handling.
Worker involvement in equipment selection, trials and training improves practical control design.

families.s: HSE control of occupational asthma and rhinitis in food production
families.t: flour, grain, egg, fish, wood, sensitisers, prevention, monitoring, health surveillance
f: Food workers can develop occupational asthma after inhaling respiratory sensitisers.
Flour and grain dust are major causes of occupational asthma in bakers and millers.
Egg and fish proteins can also act as respiratory sensitisers.
Grain, flour, spices and seasonings can cause rhinitis and eye irritation.
COSHH management should assess risk and prevent exposure where reasonably practicable.
Residual exposure should be adequately controlled and monitored.
Workers at continuing risk may require suitable health surveillance.
Low-dust flour and careful handling can materially reduce airborne exposure during dusting tasks.
